column3: Worldly disgrace is tasted before the explicitly greater punishment of the Hereafter.
It explicitly presents another punishment below or before the final one as a distinct stage.
Tasting the consequence turns a warning into direct experience, though it is not a punishment hierarchy.
Successively greater signs and punishments are administered so that the people may return.
The immediately preceding ayah identifies the Fire whose punishment the focus contrasts with the nearer one.
The command to taste the Fire's punishment parallels punishment becoming inescapably experienced.
It names the greatest punishment, clarifying the focus's greater final consequence.
Brief worldly enjoyment is followed by return and tasted severe punishment, preserving the temporal sequence.
It makes punishment a tasted consequence for wrongdoing, but lacks the lesser-to-greater sequence.
The retained idol is arranged as evidence intended to provoke return, without the punishment framework.
Its immediate context establishes death and return to the Lord, the horizon behind the greater punishment.
A worldly punishment is tasted while the punishment of the Hereafter is explicitly worse.
It contrasts presumptuous denial after mercy with a coming tasted severe punishment.
Double and great punishment indicate severity but not a corrective prior stage.
The greatness describes plotting, not punishment or return.
Destroyed neighboring towns and varied signs are presented to induce the present audience to return.
The nearby historical destructions function as signs for listeners, supporting warning before final judgment.
Those who denied the Fire first acknowledge its truth and then are commanded to taste punishment.
People are made to taste some consequences of their deeds so that they may return.
Tasting punishment confirms warnings through experience, without a stated lesser stage.
The overwhelming greatest event supplies a final counterpart to the focus's greater punishment.
Beneficial and harmful trials are given so that people may return, broadly paralleling corrective adversity.
The skeptical demand for the decisive event only loosely frames the focus's future consequence.
The greatest sign is shown as prior evidence, anticipating a later irreversible greatest event.
It directly describes tasting painful punishment but adds no corrective or staged relation.
Divine greatness here concerns God's truth and authority, not punishment.
Hell recompense for false divinity is an ultimate consequence without the focus's staged logic.
Seeing severe punishment exposes misplaced allegiance, but only at the final consequence.
Cosmic governance and ascent do not clarify the punishment or return sequence.
The failure of false gods to help does not illuminate the focus's punishment framework.
The greatest terror marks final safety for believers, not the corrective punishment of the focus.
The description of gardens is unrelated to punishment or return.
Return to Hell is a final return that contrasts with the still-open return sought in the focus.
Its repentance warning and painful punishment are related, but the greater pilgrimage is unrelated.
The denial of meeting God supplies the immediate disbelief that the focus seeks to correct.
Restricting reality to worldly life rejects resurrection, the future horizon made present in the focus.
Multiplied punishment is a final penalty without a lesser corrective stage.
Worldly life can deceive people about God's true promise, supporting the near-versus-final contrast.
Detailed signs are given expressly so that people may return, matching the focus's corrective aim.
It contrasts the lower worldly gain with the better Hereafter, though not as punishment.
Tasting eternal punishment after neglecting the meeting-day gives the final counterpart to the focus's near punishment.
Preference for worldly life over the Hereafter explains the distorted near-first outlook addressed by the focus.
Worldly idol solidarity dissolves at resurrection into mutual rejection and the Fire.
The command to taste burning punishment turns culpable speech into an experienced consequence.
Disbelief is answered by the command to taste punishment, though no lesser stage is specified.
Worldly deception culminates in painful punishment, contrasting present delusion with consequence.
The immediate preceding sign of life from barren land is evidence available before the warning's final outcome.
Turning away leads into arduous punishment, presenting punishment as a consequence of a chosen direction.
A local punishment is explicitly set beside the greater punishment of the Hereafter.
Tasting death precedes full recompense at resurrection, a broader staged temporal pattern.
Those who divert from God's way taste evil and face great punishment.
Persistent disbelief lasts until painful punishment is seen, showing recognition arriving too late.
The immediate following ayah states that faith no longer benefits on the decisive day, defining the focus's time for return.
Its false objects of worship and distant error do not clarify the punishment sequence.
Even every sign fails to move them until painful punishment is seen, when belief is too late.
The warning about Satan's party reaching the Blaze lacks the focus's staged or corrective relation.
The absence of protectors does not illuminate lesser punishment or return.
The threat of military humiliation is not the focus's punitive and eschatological sequence.
God's creative sovereignty and lack of intercessors do not clarify the focus.
The destined tasting of punishment makes prior divine warning an unavoidable experienced reality.
False gods sought for help are unrelated to the staged punishment theme.
Return from earth and emergence supports resurrection, but not corrective punishment.
It recalls punishment and warnings generally without the focus's temporal structure.
Severe prepared punishment is paired with a call to God-consciousness, retaining a warning function.
The immediate context defines the revelation as a warning intended to guide an unwarned people.
Nearness describes location and changing victory, not punishment or moral return.
An enduring word is preserved among descendants so that they may return.
The lower pair of gardens is a spatial ranking unrelated to punishment.
Arrogance and disbelief do not themselves clarify the focus's staged punishment.
It affirms a divinely owned painful punishment alongside mercy, but not its nearer corrective form.
The immediate context gives the final filling of Hell that forms the greater consequence.
It names great punishment after failed supports, without the near-stage or return purpose.
The planned return is narrative travel, not moral return after warning.
Revival of dead land illustrates resurrection but not the focus's punishment logic.
It holds worldly good and Hereafter good together while seeking protection from the Fire.
Past destroyed generations are a warning, but their non-return is not corrective return.
The contrast of divine rule with powerless objects of worship is unrelated to punishment stages.
Return to God supplies the final destination contrasted with returning while correction remains possible.
The plotted reversal of belief uses return in a different social sense.
Severe punishment is stated generically without the focus's experiential or sequential relation.
Arrogance rests on denying return to God, the denial the focus addresses before final judgment.
Fear of the Lord's punishment is not a parallel to its staged corrective administration.
Trial through evil and good before return to God broadly parallels a testing interval before final return.
The denial of being punished is relevant only as a generic stance toward punishment.
Worldly disgrace is followed by tasted burning punishment on the Day of Resurrection.
The fragile-protector analogy does not clarify punishment, tasting, or return.
Earlier communities receive hardship and adversity so that they may humble themselves.
Rescue from painful punishment is offered, but the focus's lesser corrective stage is absent.
Reminder is given so people may become mindful, without the punishment mechanism.
The nearest heaven and prepared Blaze do not establish the focus's punishment relation.
The announcement of painful punishment is a warning, but not a lesser tasted consequence.
Choosing punishment over forgiveness names a final exchange rather than corrective discipline.
It commands an embodied experience of burning punishment, without the lesser-to-greater contrast.
Knowledge confined to the worldly surface neglects the Hereafter, matching the focus's present-versus-future horizon.
Arrogant fabrication is met at death with humiliating punishment, a direct experiential consequence.
The distinction between association and forgiveness does not clarify the focus's punishment sequence.
Being returned to another religion is unrelated to moral return after punishment.
Punishment and mercy culminate in being turned back to God, supplying the final-return frame.
Scriptural distortion does not clarify punishment, tasting, or return.
Worldly gain is contrasted with the Hereafter, but without the focus's corrective punishment logic.
When punishment came, the intended response was humble return, but hardened hearts refused it.
After ignoring reminders, people are briefly given ease before sudden seizure, showing a warning window can close.
Communities are seized with hardship and adversity so that they may humble themselves.
Years of scarcity and crop loss are imposed on Pharaoh's people so that they may remember.
Successive afflictions are sent as distinct signs, yet arrogance prevents a return.
Repeated yearly trials are explicitly followed by the question why they neither repent nor remember.
Continuing calamities strike or approach the deniers until God's promise comes to pass.
Worldly punishment is explicitly paired with a harsher punishment in the Hereafter.
A secure town is made to taste hunger and fear because of its denial, making consequences directly experienced.
Tasting doubled punishment in life and at death presents punishment across successive temporal stages.
Even after being seized with punishment, they neither humbled themselves nor pleaded to their Lord.
Different peoples are seized through proportionate worldly destructions for their wrongdoing.
Pharaoh's people face an ongoing Fire before the Day when they enter the severest punishment.
A punishment is lifted for a little while, yet the people are said to return to their former rejection.
The temporary punishment gives way to the greatest seizure, an explicit lesser-to-greater escalation.
Rebellious towns are subjected to severe reckoning and terrible punishment after rejecting God's command.
They taste the evil consequence of their conduct, with loss as the final outcome.
